title: A weekly temperature variability buffer did not repeat across six coral survey samples in 1998-2019
abstract: We tested whether long-term weekly temperature anomaly variability reduced the heat response of coral bleaching. The main model used 4,625 repeated Reef Check site-month records at 1,187 sites in 1998-2019. It controlled for site, ocean-year, ocean-month, and depth. For each 0.5 C increase in anomaly standard deviation, the bleaching slope changed by -1.69 percentage points per four degree-heating weeks. Its nominal 95% interval was -2.71 to -0.66. Only the later Pacific sample gave a negative interval after correction for six ocean-period tests. The pooled same-calendar-month estimate was -0.92, with an interval of -2.61 to +0.76. Selected surveys, limited heated records, broad spatial exposure, and unknown coral composition limit inference. This test uses a weekly satellite measure, not daily reef logger variation. It cannot establish acclimation, a causal climate effect, species loss, or air pollution effects. The package includes the survey panel, code, all estimates, figures, source hashes, and numerical checks.

display.caption: Pooled heat interaction estimates under different survey and exposure restrictions. Negative values fit a buffer. Intervals are nominal 95% region-cluster intervals.
Full-period estimates and six separate ocean-period tests. The period intervals use a Bonferroni correction for six tests.

citations.reason: Adapt the published duplicate controls and fixed-effect projection method. Rebuild the panel from raw data with a new variability modifier. Observations overlap.
Prior campaign modifier test concerns turbidity. We test weekly temperature variability on overlapping surveys.
Prior global association of weekly temperature variability with lower bleaching motivates this within-site heat interaction test.
Prior daily logger study; its exposure differs from the weekly satellite measure used here.
